title: API key format
text: Nimbus API keys are 40-character strings prefixed with the environment: nmb_live_ for production and nmb_test_ for the sandbox. The prefix lets tooling detect leaked keys and route requests to the right environment.

title: Rotating API keys
text: Rotate keys from the dashboard every 90 days. After rotation the previous key keeps working for a 24-hour grace period, so deployments can be updated without downtime.

title: API key scopes
text: Every key carries read-only or read-write scopes per resource family. Grant the least privilege that works: a metrics dashboard only needs read scope on monitoring resources.

title: 401 vs 403 responses
text: HTTP 401 means the credentials are missing or invalid, while 403 means the credentials are valid but not allowed to perform the action. If you get 403 with code ERR_IP_NOT_ALLOWED, the caller IP is outside the key's allowlist.

title: Service tokens vs user tokens
text: Service tokens authenticate server-to-server jobs and never expire until revoked. User tokens carry an individual user identity and expire after 12 hours, so long-lived automation must use a service token.

title: OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow
text: Web applications should use the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE. Refresh tokens rotate on every use, and a reused refresh token revokes the whole grant.

title: Storing and leaking keys
text: Never hardcode API keys in source control; read them from environment variables or a secret manager. If a key leaks, revoke it immediately in the dashboard - revocation takes effect within 60 seconds.

title: IP allowlisting for keys
text: Enterprise keys can be restricted to specific CIDR ranges. Requests arriving from unknown IP addresses are rejected with 403 ERR_IP_NOT_ALLOWED even when the key itself is valid.

title: Personal access tokens
text: Personal access tokens (PATs) authenticate the CLI and editor plugins. They are scope-limited, tied to one user, and have a maximum lifetime of one year.

title: Per-key rate limits
text: Each API key inherits the rate limit of its plan tier; limits do not pool across keys. Enterprise customers can ask support to raise the limit on individual keys without touching the plan.

title: Default API rate limit
text: The platform allows 120 requests per minute per API key. Exceeding this rate limit returns HTTP 429 and the rejected request does not count against your quota.

title: Handling 429 with Retry-After
text: Every 429 response includes a Retry-After header in seconds. Honor it with exponential backoff and jitter instead of retrying on a fixed interval, or you will stay throttled.

title: Burst vs sustained traffic
text: Short bursts up to twice the nominal rate are absorbed for windows up to 10 seconds. Sustained traffic above the limit is throttled regardless of bursts, so averages matter more than peaks.

title: Sliding window rate limiting
text: Rate limits are enforced over a rolling 60-second sliding window, not fixed calendar minutes. Sending your whole minute of budget in the last second of one window still spills into the next.

title: Rate limit response headers
text: Responses carry X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and X-RateLimit-Reset (a unix timestamp). Use X-RateLimit-Remaining to slow down before you get a 429.

title: Requesting a quota increase
text: Standard plan quota increases require upgrading the plan. Enterprise customers can request higher limits through a support ticket that describes the workload and expected peak traffic.

title: Per-endpoint rate limits
text: Some endpoints have tighter limits: /v1/search allows 30 requests per minute. Batch endpoints count each item in the batch against the limit.

title: 429 vs 503
text: HTTP 429 means your client exceeded its quota; HTTP 503 means the service is temporarily overloaded and shedding load. Both deserve backoff, but only 429 indicates that you control the cause.

title: Sandbox rate limits
text: The sandbox (nmb_test_ keys) runs at half the production rate limits. Finish load testing in the sandbox early, because production headroom differs.

title: Webhook deliveries and rate limits
text: Webhook deliveries do not consume API rate limit budget. They have a separate delivery budget of 10,000 events per day on Pro plans.

title: 502 Bad Gateway
text: A 502 means an upstream service returned an invalid or empty response at the edge. It is usually transient: retry with exponential backoff before investigating deeper.

title: 504 ERR_GATEWAY_TIMEOUT
text: The 504 code ERR_GATEWAY_TIMEOUT is returned when an upstream service does not answer within 30 seconds. Check the status page for incidents and move long-running jobs to the async jobs API instead of holding connections open.

title: Idempotency keys
text: Attach an Idempotency-Key header to POST requests that create resources or move money. Retries after a timeout then cannot duplicate the operation; the platform stores keys for 24 hours.

title: Client retry policy
text: Retry only operations that are idempotent, or protect them with an Idempotency-Key. Use exponential backoff starting at 500 ms with a factor of 2, at most 5 attempts, plus jitter.

title: 400 vs 422 validation errors
text: HTTP 400 signals a malformed request (bad JSON, wrong types); 422 signals a syntactically valid request that fails semantic validation. Validation failures include an error.details array describing each offending field.

title: Choosing client timeouts
text: Set client timeouts above p99 latency: 10 seconds for REST calls and 60 seconds for batch endpoints. A timeout shorter than typical latency converts slow answers into spurious failures.

title: Client-side circuit breaker
text: After 5 consecutive 5xx responses, pause requests to that endpoint for 30 seconds. A simple circuit breaker keeps a degraded service from being ground down by eager clients.

title: Error response envelope
text: All errors share one envelope: error.code, error.message, error.details, and error.request_id. Always include request_id when contacting support - it pinpoints the exact hop that failed.

title: Triaging a 5xx spike
text: During a 5xx spike, check the status page first, then your region field, then the error code histogram in the dashboard. Most spikes are platform-side; the request_id in each error envelope confirms which service produced the failure.

title: Maximum response size
text: Responses larger than 10 MB are rejected with 413 ERR_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE. Paginate list endpoints instead of requesting unbounded result sets.

title: Webhook delivery guarantee
text: Webhooks are delivered at least once. Duplicate deliveries can happen, so deduplicate on the event_id field, which is stable across retries of the same event.

title: Verifying webhook signatures
text: Each delivery carries an X-Nimbus-Signature header: an HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body computed with your endpoint secret. Verify the signature against the raw bytes before parsing JSON to prevent spoofed payloads.

title: Webhook retry schedule
text: Failed deliveries are retried up to 12 times over 24 hours with exponential backoff. Your endpoint must respond with a 2xx within 5 seconds, or the attempt counts as failed.

title: Webhook event ordering
text: Events are not guaranteed to arrive in order. Compare the per-object sequence field and buffer out-of-order updates instead of assuming ordering.

title: Webhook replay protection
text: Signed deliveries include a timestamp; reject signatures older than 5 minutes to defend against replay attacks. Keep your server clock synchronized via NTP.

title: Managing webhook endpoints
text: Add and rotate webhook endpoints in the dashboard. The signing secret is displayed exactly once at creation time - store it in your secret manager immediately.

title: Sending test webhook events
text: The dashboard can send a test ping of type ping to any endpoint. Pings are not logged in the delivery log, so use them freely during development.

title: Webhook event types
text: Events follow the resource.action pattern, e.g. payment.succeeded or deploy.completed. Subscribing to the wildcard * receives every event type on the account.

title: Debugging missing webhooks
text: The delivery log retains 7 days of attempts with the response code and latency of each try. A missing event is almost always a non-2xx response or a timeout on your side.

title: Webhook endpoint auto-disable
text: Endpoints that fail 50 consecutive deliveries are disabled automatically. Re-enable them from the dashboard after fixing the root cause; backlogged events are replayed in order.

title: Python SDK versioning
text: The Python SDK major version tracks the API version it targets. Pin the exact version in your lockfile; minor releases can add fields your dataclasses must tolerate.

title: Cursor-based pagination
text: List endpoints return a next_cursor field. Pass it back as the cursor query parameter and stop when it is null; do not compute page numbers yourself.

title: SDK timeout configuration
text: SDKs default to a 10 second timeout, configurable per client. Keep it above the p99 latency of your calls or retries will multiply load.

title: TLS requirements
text: Connections require TLS 1.2 or newer; TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are rejected at handshake. The SDKs ship a pinned CA bundle, so custom trust stores are rarely needed.

title: Automatic 429 handling in SDKs
text: The SDKs retry 429 responses automatically, honoring Retry-After, up to 3 times. Set max_retries=0 if your application prefers to own throttling behavior.

title: Async SDK client
text: An asyncio-based client ships with the Python SDK for Python 3.10+. It shares the same authentication and retry machinery as the synchronous client.

title: SDK error classes
text: SDK exceptions derive from NimbusError: AuthError for 401/403, RateLimitError for 429, and APIError otherwise. Match on the class, then inspect the code attribute for the platform error code.

title: TypeScript SDK
text: The TypeScript SDK ships dual ESM/CJS builds and requires Node 18+. Responses are fully typed against the OpenAPI schema.

title: Automatic idempotency keys in SDKs
text: client.idempotent_post() generates and attaches an Idempotency-Key derived from the request payload. Use it for any POST that retries could duplicate.

title: Deprecated SDK versions
text: SDK versions get a 12-month deprecation window with security fixes only. The changelog lists the exact end-of-support date for each major version.

title: Database connection pooling
text: Managed Postgres allows 100 concurrent connections per instance. Put pgbouncer in transaction mode in front of worker fleets, and size pool_size to cores, not to workers.

title: Safe schema migrations
text: Run migrations with nimbus db migrate and follow expand-contract: add nullable columns first, backfill, then enforce constraints in a later release. Backward-compatible migrations make rollbacks safe.

title: Automated backups and PITR
text: Daily snapshots are retained for 30 days, and write-ahead logs support point-in-time recovery to any second within the last 7 days. Recovery to a chosen timestamp is a restore operation, not a manual replay.

title: Replica lag and read-your-writes
text: Read replicas replicate asynchronously with typical lag under 100 ms. Read-your-writes consistency requires reading from the primary or pinning the session to the replica it wrote to.

title: Supported Postgres versions
text: Managed Postgres supports versions 14, 15, and 16. Major version upgrades run on a new instance followed by dump-and-restore, not in place.

title: Database storage limits
text: Instances include 10 GB of storage and autoscale up to 1 TB. Overage is billed per GB-month and appears on the usage dashboard within 5 minutes.

title: Encryption at rest
text: All databases are encrypted at rest with AES-256. Enterprise customers can bring their own keys (BYOK), which are rotated without downtime.

title: Finding slow queries
text: pg_stat_statements is enabled by default; order by total_time to find the costliest queries. Most slow paths trace back to a missing index after a schema change.

title: Restoring a database to a point in time
text: Restore with nimbus db restore --to 2026-11-01T10:00:00Z --target new-instance. The restore replays WAL up to the requested timestamp onto a fresh instance.

title: Too many connections error
text: ERR_DB_CONN_LIMIT appears when the 100-connection ceiling is hit. Raise the pool limit, add pgbouncer, or scale to a larger instance class.

title: Blue-green deployments
text: Blue-green keeps two identical environments and switches the router after health checks pass on the idle one. Rolling back is flipping the router back, which takes seconds.

title: Canary releases
text: Canary releases route 5% of traffic to the new version and ramp up once error rate and latency look stable. Automated analysis compares the canary against the baseline.

title: Build cache
text: Dependency layers are cached by the hash of the lockfile, which cuts typical CI time by about 70 percent. Changing the lockfile invalidates only the layers above it.

title: Rolling back a deployment
text: nimbus deploy rollback redeploys the previous immutable artifact. Because artifacts are immutable, rollback cannot drift from what actually ran before.

title: Immutable build artifacts
text: Every build produces a content-addressed image; the same digest always means the same bytes. Deployments reference digests, never moving tags like latest.

title: Runtime secrets injection
text: Environment variables and secret references are injected at boot, never baked into images. Rotating a secret requires a restart of the affected service.

title: Health checks
text: Expose /healthz for liveness and /readyz for readiness. Failing readiness removes the instance from the load balancer without restarting it.

title: Zero-downtime deploys
text: Rolling updates are the default strategy. On shutdown the platform sends SIGTERM and waits up to 30 seconds for connections to drain.

title: Preview environments
text: Every pull request gets an ephemeral preview environment with its own URL. Previews are destroyed automatically when the PR merges or closes.

title: Build timeouts
text: Builds time out after 20 minutes. Split monorepo builds per service, or request a limit extension for release branches through support.

title: Log sampling
text: Debug-level logs are sampled at 1 percent on high-volume services; error-level logs are always kept. Sampling keeps a month of logs affordable without losing failures.

title: Trace retention and propagation
text: Distributed traces are retained for 7 days. Propagate the X-Nimbus-Trace-Id header so spans from your services join the platform's trace.

title: Metric cardinality
text: Do not use unbounded label values such as user_id or request_id as metric labels. Cardinality explosions inflate storage cost and slow every query.

title: Defining SLOs and error budgets
text: Define SLOs per user-facing journey in the SLO dashboard. Pages fire on fast burn (2 percent of budget in an hour) or slow burn (5 percent in 28 days).

title: Reducing alert fatigue
text: Page only on symptoms that hurt users; route everything else to a digest channel. Every page should be actionable - if no action exists, it is a digest.

title: Structured logging
text: Emit JSON logs with a level field and a request_id so lines can be correlated. Text logs cost the same but cannot be filtered after the fact.

title: Tail-based trace sampling
text: Tail-based sampling keeps 100 percent of traces that contain an error or exceed 500 ms. Everything else is sampled at the baseline rate.

title: Dashboards as code
text: Dashboards are defined in YAML files in your repository and synced with nimbus dashboards apply. Reviews of dashboard changes happen in pull requests, like code.

title: Log-based metrics
text: Parse rules can extract counters from logs into metrics, cheaper than shipping every line to the metrics store. Use them for high-volume events you only need as rates.

title: Audit logs
text: Admin actions land in an immutable audit log retained for one year. Stream it to your SIEM with the audit export connector.

title: VPC peering
text: VPC peering connects your cloud network to Nimbus privately, without traversing the public internet. Overlapping CIDR ranges are rejected at setup, so plan address space early.

title: Custom domains and TLS
text: Attach custom domains with a CNAME to the edge endpoint. Certificates are issued via ACME and renewed automatically; no manual uploads needed.

title: Internal DNS
text: Names under *.internal resolve only inside the same region with a 30-second TTL. They are invisible from the public internet by design.

title: Load balancer stickiness
text: The L7 load balancer supports sticky sessions by cookie or by source IP. Sticky sessions help stateful apps but can skew canary traffic splits.

title: WebSocket support
text: WebSockets terminate at the edge with a 60-second idle timeout. Send ping frames at least every 30 seconds to keep idle connections alive.

title: MTU and packet loss
text: The overlay network adds encapsulation overhead; interfaces default to MTU 1420. Large-payload packet loss over peering is usually an MTU mismatch on your side.

title: Egress IP ranges
text: Outbound traffic leaves from published IP ranges listed in the docs. Allowlist those ranges on your firewall so platform calls are not dropped.

title: VPC peering vs PrivateLink
text: Peering connects whole networks; PrivateLink exposes one service endpoint without network-level access. Prefer PrivateLink when you want a single service, not a routed network.

title: CORS configuration
text: Browser requests to custom domains need CORS rules configured at the edge. The platform adds the headers; wildcard origins are allowed only in the sandbox.

title: DDoS protection
text: L3/L4 volumetric attacks are scrubbed automatically. L7 protection uses rate-based rules you can tune per route in the dashboard.

title: Usage metering
text: Usage is metered hourly and aggregated into monthly invoices. The usage dashboard lags reality by about 5 minutes.

title: Plan tiers
text: Plans are Hobby (sandbox only), Pro, Team, and Enterprise. Enterprise adds a 99.95 percent SLA, SSO, and audit exports.

title: Proration
text: Upgrades mid-cycle are prorated to the hour; downgrades issue a credit on the next invoice. Canceling keeps the service running until the period you paid for ends.

title: Promotional credits
text: Promotional credits apply automatically to invoices before your card is charged. They expire 12 months after issuance and do not roll over.

title: Invoices and VAT
text: Invoices are issued on the first of each month and can be downloaded as PDFs in billing settings. Add your VAT ID there to have it printed on every invoice.

title: Overage policy
text: Pro plans and above use soft limits: exceeding quota produces overage billing instead of a hard cutoff. Hard stops apply only to the Hobby plan.

title: Failed payments and grace period
text: Failed card charges are retried 3 times over 7 days. After the final failure, accounts get a 14-day grace period before suspension.

title: Refund policy
text: The first invoice of a new account is refundable within 30 days. Request refunds through support; later invoices are credited case by case.

title: Enterprise procurement
text: Enterprise onboarding supports purchase orders, a security review pack (SOC 2 report), and DPA signing. Contact sales to start procurement.

title: Spend alerts
text: Set budget thresholds at 50, 80, and 100 percent to get email alerts. Crossing a threshold also emits a billing.threshold_crossed webhook event.
